claude.sample_unit: original CT oncology reports (30 colorectal, 30 lung), each simplified into two versions and rated by radiologists and PPI readers

links.outcome: PPI-rated accessibility/readability of LLM-simplified reports versus original report
links.effect: Original reports scored lower than versions A and B for accessibility (median 1.667 vs 4.333 for both); full-length version B rated higher than summary A (P=0.029); 60% (A) and 85% (B) scored >4.
links.quote: In all questions, combined colorectal and lung cohorts, the Friedman test showed significant differences between the original version, version A, and version B reports (all P < 0.0001), with the original scoring less for accessibility and being beneficial to patients, in comparison with versions A and B as per Table 4 .

links.outcome: Incorrect, misleading, or missing content in AI-simplified reports flagged by readers
links.effect: Open comments identified incorrect facts/statements (n=28), complex terminology (n=18), added confusion (n=10) and missing information (n=10) in LLM outputs.
links.quote: Incorrect facts and statements in versions A and/or B were the most common open comment ( n = 28), followed by complex terminology ( n = 18), adding confusion ( n = 10) as well as missing information ( n = 10).

links.outcome: Factual errors and potentially harmful content in AI-generated patient-facing report versions
links.effect: Radiologists found LLM reports with incorrect statements (n=28 comments); factual correctness >4 in only 65% (A) and 70% (B) of scores; harm noted in some outputs.
links.quote: Nevertheless, this study does highlight that, in some instances, the LLM generated factually incorrect or potentially harmful information which has also been highlighted by other groups [ 25 ].

links.outcome: Repeatability of LLM outputs across ten runs and repeat reads after washout
links.effect: Prompts were run ten times each and scored, giving good repeatability; repeat reads on six reports showed no significant differences between versions.
links.quote: The results gave good repeatability and the selected prompts were: Prompt A (three shot) – summary of the original report

links.outcome: Output reproducibility across repeated runs of selected prompts
links.effect: Each prompt was run ten times at temperature 0 and scored; results gave good repeatability. Reader repeatability subset showed no significant differences.
links.quote: The results gave good repeatability and the selected prompts were: Prompt A (three shot) – summary of the original report

links.outcome: Patient/public representative input in evaluating AI-simplified reports
links.effect: PPI readers (180 reads) preferred full-length version B (P<0.0001), differing from radiologist preferences in the lung cohort, showing that patient input revealed distinct preferences.
links.quote: While radiologists’ preferences differed between cohorts, with the lung cohort preferring the summary version and the colorectal cohort preferring the full-length version, patients’ overall preference was for the latter.

links.effect: Three radiologists per cohort scored outputs on 5-point Likert; radiologist scores differed per cohort (Simpson's paradox), so the study did not mitigate rater variability with adjudication.
links.quote: The differences in both cancer cohorts are cancelled when combined, a possible case of Simpson’s paradox [ 17 ], hence the importance of analysing the cohorts separately.
